question.text:
A 4-year-old girl visits the clinic to establish primary care after immigrating to the United States from Mexico 8 months ago. She is undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Her vital signs are normal, and she appears well. A review of her immunization records shows the following:

|  | Birth | 2 months | 4 months | 6 months | 12 months | 15 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hepatitis B virus | X | X |  | X |  |  |
| Rotavirus |  | X | X | X |  |  |
| Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis |  | X | X | X |  | X |
| Haemophilus influenzae type b |  | X | X | X | X |  |
| 13-Valent pneumococcal conjugate |  | X | X | X | X |  |
| Inactivated poliovirus |  | X | X | X |  |  |
| Hepatitis A virus |  |  |  |  | X |  |
| Measles-mumps-rubella |  |  |  |  | X |  |
| Varicella-zoster virus |  |  |  |  | X |  |

Which of the following vaccines should this patient receive during today's visit?
Answer Choices: (A) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and hepatitis A virus (B) Measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, and hepatitis A virus (C) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and inactivated poliovirus (D) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, inactivated poliovirus, and 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate (E) Inactivated poliovirus, measles-mumps-rubella, and varicella-zoster virus (F) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, inactivated poliovirus, measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, and hepatitis A virus (G) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, inactivated poliovirus, and hepatitis A virus (H) Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella-zoster virus (I) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, and hepatitis A virus (J) Hepatitis A virus, inactivated poliovirus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b

options.A: Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and hepatitis A virus
options.B: Measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, and hepatitis A virus
options.C: Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and inactivated poliovirus
options.D: Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, inactivated poliovirus, and 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate
options.E: Inactivated poliovirus, measles-mumps-rubella, and varicella-zoster virus
options.F: Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, inactivated poliovirus, measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, and hepatitis A virus
options.G: Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, inactivated poliovirus, and hepatitis A virus
options.I: Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, and hepatitis A virus
options.J: Hepatitis A virus, inactivated poliovirus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is 4 years old and has not received all recommended vaccines. The patient is immunocompromised due to chemotherapy. The patient is also from Mexico, which may have different vaccination schedules. The patient is due for MMR and Varicella vaccines. Hepatitis A vaccine is also recommended.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The patient is 4 years old and has not received all recommended vaccines.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Measles, mumps, and rubella are common childhood illnesses. Varicella is also a common childhood illness. Hepatitis A is a viral infection that can cause liver damage. The patient is immunocompromised, so the risk of complications from these diseases is higher. The patient is from Mexico, which may have different vaccination schedules. The patient is due for MMR and Varicella vaccines. Hepatitis A vaccine is also recommended.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is 4 years old and has missed several routine immunizations. She needs measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox), and hepatitis A vaccines as these are not documented in her record. She also needs inactivated poliovirus and diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (DTaP) boosters since her last dose was at 15 months. Hepatitis A is recommended for all unvaccinated children in the US, and she missed it at 15 months. The 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate was given at 12 months, so no repeat is needed.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Age of 4 years and incomplete immunization record showing missing MMR, varicella, hepatitis A, and polio vaccines
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether she might have medical contraindications to vaccines, but her normal vital signs and well appearance suggest she is healthy. Also considered if she might be behind on vaccines due to non-medical reasons, but the pattern of missing vaccines suggests she needs catch-up immunizations.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is a 4-year-old undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which suppresses immune function and increases infection risk. She is behind on routine vaccines, particularly measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), varicella, and hepatitis A, which are indicated at age 4-6 years. The immunization record shows she has not received MMR, varicella, or hepatitis A, and she is also due for a booster of diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (DTaP) and inactivated poliovirus (IPV) as per the CDC catch-up schedule. All these vaccines are safe and recommended for immunocompromised children under close monitoring.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: The immunization record shows the patient has not received measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster virus, or hepatitis A virus vaccines at age 4, which are indicated for catch-up at this age.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other options were ruled out because they omit critical vaccines (e.g., MMR, varicella, hepatitis A) that are essential for this age group and immunocompromised patient, or include vaccines (like pneumococcal or Hib) that are not indicated at this age or stage of treatment.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: B, E, H — these include live vaccines (measles-mumps-rubella, varicella-zoster) that are contraindicated in an immunocompromised child. The correct choice (G) provides inactivated vaccines that are safe and may be needed if she is missing any of them.
